overview.text: Jamestown is a historic settlement on Jamestown Island in Virginia, founded by the Virginia Company in 1607 as England’s first permanent settlement in North America. English colonists established it amid the homelands of Indigenous Powhatan peoples, whose interactions with the newcomers included trade, assistance, and conflict. Jamestown became Virginia’s colonial-government center; a representative assembly met there in 1619, and tobacco exports helped make the colony profitable. In 1676, Bacon’s Rebellion—a complex conflict involving political and economic grievances and escalating violence against Indigenous communities—culminated in rebels burning much of the town. In 1699, Virginia’s capital moved to Williamsburg, and Jamestown declined as an urban center.

key_facts.text: The Virginia Company’s colonists selected Jamestown on May 13, 1607; the settlement was named for King James I.
Powhatan people were important to the colony’s early survival, and relations between the communities included both cooperation and conflict.
John Rolfe introduced a tobacco strain in 1612; tobacco became an important source of profit for the Virginia Company.
Jamestown hosted Virginia’s first representative legislative assembly in 1619.
During Bacon’s Rebellion in 1676, rebels burned Jamestown; historians describe the uprising as a complex crisis, not simply a precursor to the American Revolution.
Virginia’s government moved its capital to Williamsburg in 1699.
